stories.title: It's Meta-Harness Summer
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Meta is pushing what the Latent Space crew is calling a 'meta-harness' moment — a layer of tooling built on top of existing evaluation and testing harnesses, essentially a framework for orchestrating frameworks.

↳ THE REAL STORY
If you're already running evals with something like EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness or similar tooling, the direction here is toward a standardized layer that sits above those — letting teams compose, configure, and compare across harnesses without rewriting evaluation logic from scratch. In practice, this could mean less glue code when you're benchmarking the same model across multiple eval suites, and a more reproducible path from research to production eval pipelines.
stories.considerations: The honest question here is whether another abstraction layer actually reduces complexity or just relocates it. Harness tooling already has steep learning curves and inconsistent interfaces — adding a meta-layer risks compounding that, especially if Meta's internal assumptions about eval structure don't map cleanly to how most teams have set up their own pipelines. Worth watching whether this gets real external adoption or quietly becomes another internal Meta tool that ships open-source but is only truly maintained for Meta's own use cases.

stories.title: Why the Frontier Ecosystem must be Open — Matei Zaharia and Reynold Xin, Databricks
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Databricks co-founders Matei Zaharia and Reynold Xin sat down with Latent Space to argue the case for open frontier ecosystems — specifically what infrastructure needs to exist for companies to build and run their own agent clouds at scale.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The core argument from Zaharia and Xin is that the current trajectory — where a handful of closed API providers control the model layer — creates a structural problem for enterprises that need to own their data, customize their models, and control their inference costs. Their bet is that open models (think DBRX, Llama derivatives) plus composable infrastructure will let companies run agent workloads without routing every token through OpenAI or Anthropic. For a developer building multi-agent pipelines today, this maps to a concrete choice: do you accept vendor lock-in at the model layer in exchange for convenience, or do you invest in the plumbing to run open weights on your own infra? Databricks is positioning itself as the answer to the second path — model serving, fine-tuning, and orchestration under one roof.
stories.considerations: The honest tension here is that 'open ecosystem' is also a Databricks sales pitch. Zaharia and Xin have a direct commercial interest in enterprises not consolidating on Azure OpenAI or AWS Bedrock. The open-vs-closed debate is real, but the messenger matters: Databricks needs you to believe open weights are good enough for frontier tasks, because that's what their platform is built around. Worth watching whether the agent cloud framing holds up — running reliable, low-latency multi-agent systems on self-hosted open models is still significantly harder operationally than the pitch suggests, and most engineering teams underestimate that gap until they're in production.

stories.title: Introducing MDN MCP service
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Mozilla launched an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for MDN, exposing MDN's web documentation and browser compatibility data as a tool that AI coding assistants can query directly. Source is open at github.com/mdn/mcp.

↳ THE REAL STORY
Instead of an LLM hallucinating whether a CSS property or Web API is supported in Safari 17, it can now call the MDN MCP server and get the actual browser-compat-data answer at inference time. For developers using Claude Desktop, Cursor, or any MCP-compatible client, this means CSS/JS compatibility checks become a live lookup rather than a guess baked into training weights. Simon Willison already forked the underlying browser-compat-data into his own simonw/browser-compat-db, suggesting the data layer is immediately useful beyond Mozilla's own server.
stories.considerations: The honest question is freshness cadence — browser-compat-data on GitHub updates continuously as browser versions ship, so the value of this MCP server depends entirely on how often Mozilla syncs it. A stale compatibility table is worse than a disclaimer, because it looks authoritative. Worth checking the server's data versioning before trusting it in a CI pipeline or a production compatibility gate.

stories.title: Accidental Anonymity
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Tom MacWright, developer and hiring manager, describes a pattern emerging in job applications: candidates submitting LLM-written cover letters that link to LLM-generated portfolio sites, which link to GitHub repos with LLM-generated commits throughout — a fully synthetic applicant trail.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The practical problem isn't that AI was used — it's that the signal chain is broken. A resume used to point to a portfolio that pointed to code that pointed to commit history, each layer giving a reviewer more texture on how someone actually thinks and works. When every layer is generated, the reviewer ends up knowing nothing about the person behind it. MacWright's point is blunt: he can't evaluate someone he can't see.
stories.considerations: The catch here isn't that candidates are cheating — it's that they may not realize they're hurting themselves. A fully AI-wrapped application is indistinguishable from a blank submission to anyone who knows what to look for. The open question is whether this accelerates a shift toward hiring processes that deliberately bypass the written artifact entirely — more async video, more paid take-homes, more referral-only pipelines — which would systematically disadvantage people without existing networks, the exact candidates AI tooling was supposed to help.
